images.caption: This painting is a good example of the distinctive Kandyan Style. Here, kneeling figures adore a series of Buddhas seated in meditation. The artist has individualized both the expressions of the Buddhas and the figures of the worshipers; each pair is individually numbered and captioned. The numbers are written using the familiar Arabic numerals (9, 10, 11, etc.), and the captions are in Sinhalese.
images.alt: This painting is a good example of the distinctive Kandyan Style. Here, kneeling figures adore a series of Buddhas seated in meditation. The artist has individualized both the expressions of the Buddhas and the figures of the worshipers; each pair is individually numbered and captioned. The numbers are written using the familiar Arabic numerals (9, 10, 11, etc.), and the captions are in Sinhalese.

images.caption:
The portrait of the crowned and captioned standing king is rendered, like the other paintings in the temple, in Kandyan style. The figure
is very thick, with strangely boneless arms and short legs, although some of this may be an artifact of the elaborate and impressively padded costume that he is wearing. The king is standing underneath an honorific makara torana, and grasps a lotus stem in his right hand like a Bodhisattva. His left hand holds a piece of cloth, presumably a royal attribute.

images.caption:
A part of the complicated form and exuberant painted decoration of the temple's bracketing is seen here in close-up. It includes fanciful
animals, birds, and humans, and is located above the entrance porch to the Tooth Relic Shrine.

images.caption: After an exchange of gifts of precious stones, gold rings and a letter from the Kandy king expressing ‘friendship of his friends and enmity of his enemies’, Spilbergen made the long, treacherous journey to meet King Vimaladharmasuriya in Kandy. As Spilbergen made his way from Matelaco to Kandy, he observed numerous Buddhist pagodas, statues, ceremonies and religious architecture. The envoys travelled through the town of Vintane, which is marked on Zelon with a small pagoda. In Vintane they were greeted ‘by men with pipes, drums, horns and other musical instruments’, illustrated in a plan of the town. In the engraving, Spilbergen and his men approach from the river in the foreground. Musicians, monks, soldiers and elephants process through the streets towards the focal point– a large pagoda in the town’s centre. The text vividly describes a ‘very beautiful and high’ pagoda that is ‘all white with a gilded top and built like a pyramid, rising upwards oval wise up to a four-cornered point’. It moves from a description of the pagoda to the monastery, marked with an ‘8’ in the top right corner. The monastery is described as ‘similar to those of ours in this country, surrounded by galleries and many private chapels which are gilded and contain many gures of men and women whom they say have lived holy lives. These carved gures stand adorned with cloths painted silver.’
